First Chapter. The Goddess said:

O God of gods, Lord of the universe, omniscient one, ocean of compassion! From your gracious self, various kinds of Dharmas have been heard, which were previously established for the followers of Śiva and are in accordance with the continuous stream of the Vedas. || 1 ||

Indeed, you previously declared with a soul constrained by compassion that the Vīraśaiva dharmas are the highest of all dharmas. Desiring to hear them today, I pray that you, being gracious, explain them in their entirety.
Mahādeva said:
"Well asked by you, O Goddess, with a mind intent on the welfare of the worlds!
Indeed, I shall declare to you the duties approved by Śambhu."
O Goddess who bestows immediate liberation, [I offer] these means for my own realization of knowledge.
Regarding the undertaking of the Śāmbhava vow:
this vow called Śāmbhava, which is sanctioned by the Upaniṣads, one who desires liberation should perform it for the sake of abandoning rebirth. (4)
Whether he be a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or an ascetic, or even a woman—if she desires immediate liberation, she should embrace [this teaching]. (5)
There exists nothing equal to this, whether in the Vedas or elsewhere;
he who desires immediate liberation should observe this vow. (6)
One who desires to cross the ocean of births should take refuge in the boat of the Guru;
having thoroughly examined him, the best of teachers should accept the disciple.
Intending to impart my knowledge, one should first administer the head-vow (śirovrata);
otherwise, both the teacher and the disciple fall into the ocean of hell.
It is celebrated in the Upaniṣads by these meritorious names: Atyāśrama, Pāśupata, Śāmbhava, and Śirovrata.
Regarding the instruction on the three initiations:

having completely burned away the three impurities (mala) residing in the three bodies— the *anādi* [beginningless], the *māyīya*, and the *kārmika*— by means of the three initiations, this Guru should teach the three *liṅgas*.
The preceptor, a treasury of compassion, shall perform for the disciple standing before him the great Śaiva initiation that severs the bonds of ignorance. (11)
The connection with the *liṅga* is bestowed and the three impurities are destroyed;
because it bestows and destroys, it is called *dīkṣā*.
That supreme Śaiva initiation is threefold and stainless:
one is directly of the nature of piercing (vedha), another is considered to be of the nature of mantra, and a certain third is of the nature of ritual action (kriyā); thus it is threefold.
From the contact of hand and head, it is proclaimed that the impurity is destroyed;
for when uttered by the Guru into the ear, it becomes the essence of mantra. That initiation which is placed upon the palm of the disciple’s hand is the ritual initiation (kriyā-dīkṣā). || 14 ||
In this regard, each one of these is renowned and adorned by a set of seven initiations;
I shall explain their method, so listen with a one-pointed mind. (15)

p. 4) The Procedure for Constructing the Mandapa: Here, the preceptor, intending to initiate a disciple who possesses the previously mentioned characteristics, should diligently collect the requisite materials and their constituent parts at the appropriate time.
One should cause a pavilion to be constructed; I shall duly describe its characteristics as they are.
One should construct a pavilion for the purpose of initiation, provided with sixteen pillars, measuring either ten *sūryahastas* or eight *nṛpahastas*.
They know that the height of these pavilions should be five cubits;
they should be square, with four doors, and adorned with four archways.
To its east is a nyagrodha tree, to the south an udumbara,
to the north an aśvattha, and to the west there should be a plakṣa.
In the center of one-ninth of the nine parts, one should fashion an altar (vedī),
one cubit in height and resembling the surface of a mirror.
One should fashion there nine, five, or even just one sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa);
that in the east should be square, and that in the southeast like a pipal leaf.
In the southern direction there shall be a half-moon, while in the south-west there is a triangle;
in the western quarter it shall be circular, and in the north-west a hexagon.
There should be a lotus in the northern part, and an eight-cornered [figure] in the northeast;
between the northeast and the east, there should be either a circle or a square. (23)
One should arrange [the seats] starting from Indra and ending with Soma in the northeast;
they are square, half-moon, circular, lotus-shaped, and round.
One should prepare a single fire-altar (ekāgni-vedikā) in the east, the north, or the west, or alternatively,
one may fashion it as a square or a circle in the northeast.
Or else, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) measuring one cubit in size,
with a height of nine finger-breadths, made either of sand or clay;
having thus constructed the pavilion, one should adorn it with banners and other ornaments.
With canopies of pearl nets, with fruits, sprouts, and lotuses;
with plantain trees, garlands of darbha grass, mirrors, and incense sticks.
There, the wise one should draw the Gaurīlatāliṅga-maṇḍala using powders endowed with five colors, or else with white pigments.
Regarding the procedure for initiation:
having bathed, wearing sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads, and having consecrated his body with the kalās,
the Guru, together with the devotees of Maheśvara, should proceed to the pavilion of the disciple.
Having sprinkled the doors with the weapon-mantra (astra), one should worship those four [doors] as follows:
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the door known as the Śāntikalā"; and also, "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the door known as the Vidyākalā. || 30 ||
"Hā& obeisance to the door named Nivṛttikalā; Hā& obeisance to the door named Pratiṣṭhākalā"—
having thus worshipped those starting from the east, one should then place [the deities] upon their respective branches.
And Nandin, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgin,
Vināyaka, Vṛṣa, Skanda, and likewise the god Caṇḍa— two each in all four [directions].
Having performed three claps with the Astra-mantra, and likewise having struck the ground three times with the heel of the left foot, one should diligently drive away all obstacles.
Having opened the doors with the weapon-mantra, the wise one should enter from the western door and, having looked upon the implements of sacrifice within; 34.
Surrounded by a rampart of missiles and enveloped in armor,
one should sit comfortably upon a seat prepared with kusha grass and other materials.
Then that disciple, having taken the vessel containing betel, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and the ashes, should speak thus in the presence of the true guru: || 36 ||
"Immersed in the ocean of saṃsāra, agitated by the fear of the crocodiles of birth, wretched and subject to the noose of death—out of compassion, favor me!
Having thus made this petition, one should place that vessel before [the deity] and pay homage. (37)
The Guru, having brought that vessel and placed it in the midst of the assembly,
and having received the permission of the assembly, sat down upon his seat once more.
Intending to initiate [the disciple] here, the preceptor, having declared the place and time, should perform the worship of Gaṇeśa and the recitation for well-being and the auspicious day. (39)
Having again paid homage to the Gaṇas and proclaimed the place and time,
[he should act] for the sake of removing the three impurities residing within the three bodies.
And for the sake of attaining the fitness to contemplate the three genders,
one should perform the Śāmbhava vow preceded by the purification of the six paths (ṣaḍadhva-śuddhi).

Having formed the intention, "I shall initiate this disciple through the sevenfold initiation according to the procedure for the descent of power (śaktipāta)," one should bestow the seven initiations that constitute the intermediate rites.
The Ājñopamā, the Kaśābhiṣeka, followed by the Svastikārohaṇa, the Bhūtipaṭṭa,
and the Svāyatta— these seven are considered the intermediate initiation rites (kriyādīkṣā). || 43 ||
"Having abandoned right conduct, do not ever engage in [wrongdoing].
Having thus instructed him with the initiation of command (*ājñādīkṣā*), the Guru should then speak as follows: (44)

Having clearly instructed [the disciple] with the words, "Act in accordance with the conduct performed by the ancients," and having pointed this out through the initiation of the comparison, he should, for the sake of removing the disciple's sins,
perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) according to the rules and prepare the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
For the purpose of the five glorious jars (pañcakalaśa), the Guru should choose officiating priests;
there shall be four principal teachers for the four [directions], and he himself shall be the one for the center.
And one should invoke Īśāna in the central jar, Sadyojāta in the east, and Vāmadeva in the south. (47)
Then, having invoked the Tatpuruṣa in the north and the Aghora in the west with their respective mantras, one should worship them immediately thereafter.
(9) Having prepared a maṇḍala in the northern part of the pavilion for the preliminary consecration of the water (jalādhivāsana),
one should then extract the Śiva-liṅga, which is characterized by the five threads (pañcasūtra).
Having placed it in a copper vessel and having proclaimed the place and time, [this is done] for the pacification of the defects produced by the acts of rubbing and so forth. (50)
Immediately thereafter, one should consecrate it with the recitation of the sections beginning with "hiraṇyaśṛṅga," in their proper sequence, while saying, "I bathe the Śiva-liṅga."
One should consecrate the chosen liṅga with the perfected five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and also with the pure five nectars (pañcāmṛta), using the supreme mantras of the five Brahmās.
Having bathed that image again with pure water,

the preceptor should place it in another vessel and, having set it down upon a lotus mandala in the southwest, the most excellent preceptor should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. || 53 ||
Then, for the sake of pacifying the heat born from friction with sandpaper and other materials,
[one should place it] in a Varuṇa-maṇḍala filled with a prastha measure of water.
Having placed that liṅga, wrapped in cloth, into a copper vessel,
one should then perform the ritual immersion in water (jalādhivāsana) with mantras containing the word "water" (ab-liṅga).
Having lifted that liṅga from the water and placed it in the bathing vessel,
one should then set that vessel down in the mandala located in the northwest corner.
Having bathed the liṅga with the five products of the cow, as well as with ashes and scented water, using the mantras prescribed for that purpose, and having rubbed it dry with a cloth; 57.
Having placed that vessel into another vessel and set it within the lunar disc,
the preceptor should then worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
One should perform the consecration of grain for the manifestation of the seven elements; indeed, one should perform the ritual consecration of grain.
O Goddess, listen as I shall explain that procedure in brief. (59)
On the southern mandala, one should [arrange] rice measured by a *prastha* in sequence, then half that amount of *taṇḍula* grains, and likewise half that amount of sesame seeds. (60)
Having carefully arranged the sacrificial altars one above the other,
and having covered that linga with darbha grass, it should be placed face down with its head toward the east.
Having placed the perfumes and other offerings there with the *tatpuruṣa* mantra,
and having placed *darbha* grass upon the liṅga, one should then place the water-pots in its eight directions.
Having invoked the eight lords of the sciences (aṣṭavidyeśvara) within them and worshipped them thoroughly,
one should cover them with cloths and then perform the rite of the mouth of the Śiva-fire.
Having removed the *liṅga* from its bed and placed it in the mandala situated in the direction of fire (the southeast),
one should bathe it with the Rudra-sūkta; thereafter,
having deposited it in the mandala located in the eastern direction, one should worship it.
Then, taking that linga and placing it in the northeast corner of the mandala,
one should immerse it in another vessel and bathe it with the five Rudra mantras using the water from the jars of the mandala consecrated for the overnight ritual (adhivāsa) of the grains.
p. 12) Thereafter, one should perform the ritual of the placement of the paths (*adhvanyāsa*) and so forth, according to the rules, for the purpose of invoking the digit of Śiva (*śivakalā*).
Here, one should first form the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and then perform all six placements of the paths upon the *liṅga*.
One should place the path known as the worlds (bhuvana) upon the lower band;
however, the path of the feet and the path of the phonemes (varṇa) should be placed within that lotus, in its center.
One should then place the path of *kalās* in the upper lotus and likewise on the band;
thereafter, having placed the path of *tattvas* in the *ājya-praghārikā*,
one should worship the path of *mantras* with perfumes and other offerings.

The wise practitioner should perform the installation of the fire and other elements, and for the sake of achieving stability in their respective kalās, he should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with a total number of three hundred and twenty-four [oblations].
Likewise, again with the five-syllable mantra together with the *satīra*.
One should offer oblations of clarified butter into the principal fire-pit with the *vyāhṛtis* and with the *jaya* mantras and others; immediately thereafter, one should protect the fire.
Summoning the gentle disciple, he says, "O gentle one, sit down here," upon a tortoise-seat (kūrma-āsana) prepared with kuśa grass and other materials.
Having seated [the disciple] upon a seat with the five supreme Brahma-mantras,
and having first performed the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*) along with the regulation of breath (*prāṇasaṃdhāraṇa*) and other practices,
one should then purify the body and subsequently perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśodhana*). (72)
The preceptor should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa upon the body of the disciple;
then, he should effect the internal purification of the disciple with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Then the supreme guru should bestow the initiation of consecration upon the disciple for the sake of pacifying all defects accumulated throughout beginningless existence.
He should also bathe the disciple with pure water from five jars,
while reciting the mantras of the five Brahmās for the sake of purifying the five elements.
Then the preceptor, having removed the thread tied to the five jars,
should fasten the bracelet upon the disciple's hand while reciting the mantra "viśve tvā" (RV 10.85.47).

One should bestow, according to the prescribed rule, the initiation known as *svastikārohaṇa* for the purpose of purifying the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvaśodhana*) by means of the purification of the six paths, so that the mass of flesh may cease to exist. (77)

Following the sequence of reabsorption, the wise one should project the six paths— the nature of which consists of sound and meaning— upon the feet and other limbs of the disciple whose mind is restrained.
The wise one should place the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*), which is the form of sound, upon the two feet;
immediately thereafter, he should place the path of kalās (*kalādhvan*), which is the form of meaning, upon the penis. (79)
Having placed the path of words, which is the form of sound, at the navel, the preceptor, remaining alert, should place the path of principles, which is the form of meaning, in the heart. (80)
Having thus deposited the path of mantra, which consists of sound, in the mouth, one should likewise deposit the path of worlds, which consists of meaning, upon the head as well. (81)

Then, the preceptor, being self-restrained, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the six syllables six times upon the six locations beginning with the feet and ending with the crest-lock; 82.
One should perform the wearing of sacred ash and rudrākṣas for the removal of beginningless impurity through the initiation known as the *bhūtipaṭṭa*; furthermore,
one should cause the bathing, the smearing with ash (*uddhūlana*), and the wearing of the ash to be performed.
Then, one should wear rudrākṣa beads in sequence upon the locations beginning with the tuft of hair (śikhā).
Having consecrated a single rudrākṣa and worshipped it according to the prescribed rite,
one should tie it on the right hand of the disciple for the sake of liberation from bondage.
For the removal of the three impurities— āṇava and the others— residing in the body of the disciple,
one should indeed perform oblations with ghee using the five-syllable mantra, which consists of three hundred and twenty-four syllables and is joined with the *tāraka* (the *praṇava*).
Having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* and likewise with the *jaya*-mantras and others in due order,
and having performed the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should transfer the fire into the lotus of the disciple’s heart by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā* and then cover the two maṇḍalas.
In the first maṇḍala, one should offer the bali-oblation beginning with Rudra and ending with Kṣetrapāla;
and in the second, one should cast the bali-oblation beginning with Mahendra and ending with Maheśa.
Immediately thereafter, the Guru should bestow the initiation known as Āyatta.
The initiation [is of two kinds]: dependent initiation and self-dependent initiation.
It is marked by five lines cast upon the central mandala, known as Śānteśvara, and adorned with the placement of all mantras.
Having taken up the chosen liṅga and worshipped it in the left hand, one should show the chosen liṅga while saying, "O gentle one, behold this liṅga. || 89 ||
Then, having had the cloth shown to the preceptor and the disciple amidst the sounds of auspicious powder-sprinkling and musical instruments, they should recite the Maṅgalāṣṭaka.
Then, with the followers of Maheśvara, the teacher addressed the disciple:
"Be forever possessed of the Liṅga, firm in all three limbs."
Saying "p. 16)," while removing the curtain, he should cast auspicious unhusked rice grains upon the head of the disciple with the mantra *dhruvaṃ te*. (92)
Seating the disciple on his own seat to the left side while facing north,
he should bestow upon him the initiation known as *svāyatta*.
Then the Guru, covering both the disciple and himself with a cloth,
should consecrate the disciple’s left hand with the root mantra.
Having worshipped it well seven times, he should place that liṅga, held in his own left hand, there while recollecting the *triyambaka* mantra; thereafter,
he should also bestow those seven initiations, beginning with the *samaya*.
Initiation is of seven kinds:
the first is known as the *samaya* (vow); the second is that which is free from saṃsāra;
the third is called *nirvāṇa*; and the fourth is known as *tattva*. || 96 ||

The fifth is the internal perception (adhyātmasaṃjñā), the sixth is the purifier of reality (tattvaviśodhinī), and the seventh is the awakening to reality (tattvabodhā); these are the initiations (dīkṣās) intermediate to the piercing (vedha).

Having performed the breath-control (prāṇāyāma), the Guru, having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) "I shall perform these seven [rites] beginning with the initiation into the pledges (samaya-dīkṣā)," and having worshipped the disciple's head, [proceeds]. (98)

Having consecrated his own right hand six times with the six-syllable mantra, and having visualized it as the Hand of Śiva, he should place it upon the head of the disciple and recite [the mantra] with a one-pointed mind. (99)
Looking at the disciple while reciting the mantra "This is my hand," the wise teacher should address him as "O disciple! and speak thus. (100)
"Abandoning affection for kinsmen, establish that same steadfast love toward your devotees.
Having thus prescribed this rule, one should instruct them so that they become free from the cycle of worldly existence. (101)
Initiation is free from saṃsāra; having abandoned the cycle of the body, senses, and so forth, always contemplate in your mind: "The ritual service of worship is itself saṃsāra."
Having thus instructed [him], he bestowed the initiation known as Nirvāṇa.

With effort, do not set your mind upon this wretched end of a miserable existence, which arises from the three impurities, is agitated by the fear of the three sufferings, and is difficult to traverse.
Having thus pointed out Nirvāṇa, one should bestow that which expresses the ultimate reality.
(18) "Having understood the reality of the *liṅga* and the *aṅga*, may you attain union with the *liṅga* through the initiation into reality (*tattvadīkṣā*).
Having instructed him thus, he should then bestow that which is known as the 'inner self' (*adhyātma*). (104)
Having established the *liṅga* within the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through internal initiation, and having placed the vital breath within the *liṅga*,
remain forever one whose life-force is the *liṅga*, while gazing steadily upon the *liṅga*.
Having thus instructed, one should then bestow that which consists of the purification of reality (tattvasaṃśodhana). || 105 ||
In the initiation for the purification of reality (tattvasaṃśodhanadīkṣā),
one should offer all objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest, which fall within the range of their respective faculties, to the six types of liṅgas, headed by the ācāra-liṅga.
The initiation known as Tattvabodha (Awakening to Reality) is this:
remain forever pure-minded, self-restrained, and with senses conquered.
Having thus instructed him, one should also bestow the instruction on the principles (tattva).
The Guru, who knows the ritual procedure and is overcome by compassion, should bestow initiation. || 107 ||
"That which is designated as Brahman—the sign (liṅga) whose innate form is truth, consciousness, and bliss—you are that; therefore, meditate upon it, being certain that 'I am indeed that.
Having thus instructed the disciple with this initiation known as Awakening (bodha), the teacher [should proceed]. || 108 ||
(19) Having restrained the vital breaths (prāṇāyāma), the Guru, desiring to perform the initiation into the mantra,
shall bestow the sevenfold initiation beginning with one-pointedness of mind, in due order. (109)
Among those, the first is Ekāgramati, the second is Dṛḍhavratā, and the third is proclaimed as Pañcendriyārpaṇā. (110)

The fourth is called non-violence (ahiṃsā), while the fifth is established in the liṅga. The sixth is designated as the immediate dissolution of the mind into the liṅga, and the seventh is proclaimed as that which is termed immediate liberation (sadyomukti). || 111 ||
I shall explain its true nature; listen, O Goddess, in brief.
"Do not look upon any reality other than the chosen *liṅga*, my disciple"—having thus bestowed one-pointed attention, he should grant the initiation characterized by firm vows. (112)
"Do not abandon even your vows until the fall of your body.
Having said, "O you of firm vows," he should offer the dedication of the five senses. (113)
"Having resolved in one's mind, 'My husband is truly the Liṅga,' always offer your body, mind, and dispositions to him, even in the face of undesirable things and the like.
Having thus instructed, the Guru should then bestow that which is known as non-violence (ahiṃsā). (114)
Having instructed that one should regard all these beings as oneself and not harm them, one should then instruct [the student] in the state of being established in the *liṅga*. (115)
"Be established in that which is called Brahman— the sign (liṅga) devoid of beginning, middle, and end;
thus being a true knower," having so instructed,
the true guru should further impart the initiation consisting of the dissolution of the mind into the form of the sign.
"Contemplating the form of the Liṅga, remain for a long time without mental activity (amanaska).
Having thus instructed him, he should further bestow that which is called "Immediate Liberation" (sadyomukti).
"The procedure for the instruction of the mantra:
with a steady mind regarding the meaning spoken by me, proceed without doubt.
Having thus addressed him, that guru should recite these two mantras.
And it is clearly stated by the word of Śiva: "Within the vital breaths. (118)
Having thus instructed the six-syllable mantra three times slowly into the right ear of the disciple, he should be purified by this initiation through the mantra.
Then, having meditated upon the Śiva-kalā with one's own mind,
and having brought it forth by sight, one should quickly place it upon the liṅga held in the left hand of the disciple, while recollecting the root mantra.
As is the digit, so is existence; as is existence, so is the mind;
as is the mind, so is the view; as is the view, so is the ground. (121)
Just as a drop of oil pervades the tip of a water-filled jar, so too does the Śāmbhavī kalā abide, perfectly pervading the body, the vital breaths, and the self. 122.
Resplendent with the luster of the blazing fire of time and possessing a brilliance equal to ten million flashes of lightning,
there is above that a subtle crest, which is the supreme digit whose nature is consciousness.
Having drawn forth that supreme, most subtle digit (kalā) which awakens the principles (tattvas), one should install it upon the liṅga according to the rule;
one should also recite the mantra for the installation of life-force (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) and the root mantra (mūlamantra). || 124 ||
"Therefore, remain forever firmly established in this consecrated linga;
furthermore, I entreat you: may you become one whose body is solely devoted to me. (125)

Having instructed the disciple, saying, "May you not remain a material being, but become a being of the subtle body (liṅga-prāṇī)," he should then bestow the water from his feet and the sacred prasāda.
(22) Furthermore, the true Guru, a treasury of compassion, instructs the disciple:
"Worship the devotees of Maheśvara, the Guru, and the Liṅga properly and constantly. (127)
O one of great intelligence, apply yourself with diligence to faith regarding the eight obscurations, and proceed gradually through the five modes of conduct as well. (128)
Having addressed [the disciple] with "The initiation for the installation of the limb-liṅga," and having again restrained his breath,
the preceptor [performs] the initiation known as the installation of the limb-liṅga for the wise disciple. (129)

Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), "I shall perform [it]," and having bound the sectarian mark (liṅga) while wearing clean garments, he should recite this mantra of steadfastness: "Obeisance to Brahman" (namo brahmaṇe). || 130 ||
Immediately thereafter, one should tie it around the neck or hand of the disciple;
then, one should not discard the garment that covered the teacher and the resident student.
Instruction on the Duties of the Disciple:
Then that disciple should perform three prostrations before the Guru; he should satisfy the Preceptor with great gifts such as cows, land, and other valuables. (132)
O Goddess, this vow which bestows immediate liberation has been proclaimed by me; listen, for it bestows immediate liberation even among the infinite and extensive Vedas and Āgamas.
There exists no means for liberation superior to this. || 133 ||

For one who is devoted to the Śrauta and Smārta rites and to the conduct of the virtuous throughout infinite births, devotion directed toward other deities arises through the purification of the mind. (134)
For one whose mind has been occupied with the worship of another deity throughout infinite births, devotion toward me arises through the grace of that other deity. (135)
Even for an embodied being devoted to my worship, after many births,
it is attained by my grace that someone reaches their final birth.
By the grace of the preceptor, one who has obtained this vow through the greatness of that vow—
neither Māyā binds him, nor is he born again. 137.
For one whose bonds have been entirely burnt away by the fire of the Guru’s awakening, how could there be rebondage for that person whose fetters have been utterly consumed? (138)
For one who delights in tasting the nectar-like essence of the Guru’s compassion, how can death approach this immortality? (139)
(24) For him whose vision shines with the supreme knowledge bestowed by his guru, how could darkness ever come from the presence of that sun? 140.
How could there be sorrow for that great-minded and learned one, who is swollen with the joy of being beyond destruction and is eternally satisfied? (141)
Only he who possesses supreme faith in my spoken word as revealed in the Śruti shall be qualified for this; no other is fit for liberation.
"Thus, O Goddess, I have declared the characteristics of the Śāmbhava vow; it must be guarded with great effort. What more do you wish to hear? (143)

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Great Pāśupata Rite," in the Kriyāpāda of the Śrī Kāraṇagama, in the Uttara-bhāga, within the dialogue between the venerable Parvatī and the Supreme Lord. || 1 ||
The second chapter. The Goddess said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O Lord of the universe, salutations be unto you!
O Maheśvara, by hearing this, I have accomplished my purpose.
O Moon-crested Lord, a certain doubt arises within me here;
dispel it out of compassion, O Master of my life, and listen to my words. (2)
Previously, it was stated by you that liberation arises from knowledge alone;
how then can it be said that liberation occurs through this vow?
If liberation for embodied beings were not possible without knowledge, tell me truly: what fruit would there be from the performance of vows? (4)
Mahādeva said:
"O Goddess, you have asked well; liberation comes from knowledge alone. I shall speak; listen attentively."
"But liberation comes from knowledge alone—this is my true word. (5)
Nevertheless, the attainment of knowledge cannot occur without the vow (vrata).
Indeed, the instruction of knowledge in its entirety is said to be contained within this vow.
Without this vow, one is not qualified for knowledge. (6)
In a person who has not been refined by initiation and whose heart is agitated by impurity,
even the knowledge that has been taught does not take root, just as a seed does not grow in a desert.
Knowledge acquired with great difficulty, if it is devoid of steadfastness in the [true] mark,
will certainly not bear fruit, just like a crop that is unprotected.

When the mind of a living being has been thoroughly purified by the consecration of initiation (dīkṣā), my supreme knowledge—concealed within steadfast devotion (man-niṣṭhā) and known as the state of aesthetic identity between the Linga and the body—is watered by devotion; it certainly leads to liberation. || 9 ||
Without my grace, there is no liberation from the bonds of worldly existence;
and without my knowledge, my grace will not come to pass.
The initiation is the means for attaining knowledge;
indeed, my knowledge does not arise at all without this initiation.
Therefore, this great initiation is certainly the bestower of liberation.

Therefore, O Goddess, a living being who desires liberation, if they depart by other paths while abandoning this initiation (*dīkṣā*), does not attain release even in hundreds of millions of aeons. Thus, without doubt, this vow (*vratam*) bestows liberation. (12)
The Goddess said:
O Lord, here again a great doubt arises within me.
For it has been stated by you that initiation bestows liberation through the gateway of knowledge.
Therefore, it is established that initiation is indeed the supreme means for attaining knowledge.
If there were anyone who had been initiated yet was devoid of right knowledge and bound by attachment and aversion, how could liberation come about for him? (14)
If even he were to attain liberation, then the requirement for knowledge would be purposeless;
yet there can be no liberation for him [if that were so]. This vow does not bestow liberation.
O abode of the ocean of compassion, sever this doubt of mine! 15.
Mahādeva said:
"O Goddess, you have asked appropriately; I am pleased with your speech.
Today I shall tell you a secret that will remove your doubt."
The Śāmbhava vow is a means for attaining knowledge:
"Even for one who is ignorant or crooked, if he practices the Śāmbhava vow, [liberation] is certain at the moment of the departure of the vital breath, just as it is in Vārāṇasī. (17)
I shall impart the knowledge that makes one understand my true nature;
by that, indeed, a living being is liberated through my grace—of this there is no doubt.
Whether receiving this initiation or dwelling in the Forest of Bliss (Ānandakānana),
a person shall not fear the bondage of death, even if they act according to their own desires.
For one who follows the vow of Śambhu, even if he is averse to [higher] knowledge, there is neither the torment of birth nor the torment of restraint. (20)
Even one who is burdened with great sins attains purity once initiated;
however, an initiate who remains a sinner shall go to the torment of Bhairava.
Having thus experienced that fierce and terrible torment,
he shall become a recipient of my grace and shall not be subject to rebirth again.
Whether initiated or uninitiated, if one should be a reviler of the Śaiva conduct or a censurer of devotees and the like, he shall go to hell for an imperishable duration of time. (23)
For it was said by me, O Goddess, that initiation bestows liberation;
indeed, O Daughter of the Mountain, no doubt should be entertained regarding my word.
The Goddess said:
"O Most Auspicious One, my transgression must be forgiven; salutations be unto you!
When you are pleased, what is difficult to obtain in this world? (25)
O Bhavodbhava, I have no doubt regarding what you have said;
yet, is there any doubt concerning the Śruti? For that, too, is indeed your own well-spoken word.
Nevertheless, I questioned you with the desire to dispel the doubts of the people;
now that they have become free from uncertainty, O Bull-vehicled One, forgive me.
Mahādeva said:
"In your questioning out of a desire to favor the people, there is not even the slightest fault; rather, there would be great merit."
Ask whatever you wish, O daughter of the mountain; I shall speak.
The Goddess said:
"This very initiation of Śambhu is that which establishes one in the state of knowledge;
for the state of being established in knowledge is seen to be appropriate only for the ascetic. (29)

O ocean of compassion, tell me how the steadfastness in knowledge can be achieved by a householder whose mind is intent on daily and occasional rites, and whose thoughts are preoccupied with the maintenance of his family. (30)
Mahādeva said:
"While all are entitled to the pursuit of knowledge,
how is it that in this world only the ascetic (yati) is authorized for liberation?"
Whether he be a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or an ascetic. || 31 ||
Whether a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or even one born of the lowest caste;
whether a man, a woman, or a eunuch—all are entitled to liberation.
Whoever is a vessel for my grace is fit for liberation;
this vow does not appeal to one who is devoid of my favor.
O lady of excellent vows, liberation cannot be accomplished by anyone without knowledge;
and knowledge, in turn, cannot exist without this vow dedicated to Śambhu.
(31) This vow is of two kinds: Vedic and Tantric; thus this vow is twofold.
The Vedic is declared for the twice-born, while the Tantric is remembered for others. (35)
Whatever action is performed by a householder, whether it be obligatory or occasional, with the intention of propitiating Me, that is a means for attaining knowledge. (36)
Whatever practice of worshipping the stationary and moving liṅgas exists on earth,
it is prescribed for the family as the supreme means to liberation.
Neither that karma nor the household life obstructs the path to liberation for the wise householder who is preeminent in his devotion to the *liṅga*. 38.
How may an ascetic become a fit vessel to attain the majesty of the overflowing bliss derived from serving the multitude of my devotees, even as a householder might? (39)
If one is dispassionate, he should become a renunciant; if he is not dispassionate, he should remain a householder.
If one who is a renunciant is not dispassionate, he goes to hell for an inexhaustible time.
Even while living as a householder, attached to wife and children and lacking dispassion, if one’s mind is joined in devotion to Me, he will certainly become liberated. (41)
(32) Knowledge is declared to be the giver of liberation; the stage of life (āśrama) is not the means for attaining liberation.
For whoever possesses steadfastness in knowledge, preceded by the vow of Śambhu—be they anyone whatsoever in this world—they are indeed released from bondage. 42.
Therefore, this vow has been declared as the supreme means for liberation.
Ask further than this; what else do you wish to hear?
The Goddess said:
"How can there be eligibility for women here?
For how could this vow be performed by women?"
Whether before or after the marriage ceremony, [this] must be performed.
How could women be eligible for Vedic ritual acts at the outset? Their eligibility [for such acts] arises only from being consecrated by marriage suitable for them. (45)
If it is received later from the husband or from someone else, the initiation of Śambhu is still received; for if he is the husband, he is indeed the Guru.
The teacher would be his father; how then could this woman be his wife?
If she were from another [lineage], she would have come under the dominion of another.
Furthermore, she must abide by the word of her husband or her teacher. (47)
(33) It is said that women do not possess the authority to form a formal resolve (saṅkalpa);
for how then could they have the qualification for this initiation? || 48 ||
O Lord, how can a wife find an opportunity for knowledge when her mind is never at rest due to incessant household duties? (49)
For one who is devoted to the ultimate goal of the *liṅga*, how can there be the protection of sons and others?
Or how can there be service to the husband, and how can there be the protection of sons and others? (50)
"For women, the husband alone is the supreme deity;
tell me, how could the worship of a separate deity be appropriate for them? (51)
Mahādeva said:
The manner of receiving initiation for women is now being described; this observance is necessary even for women.
Indeed, after the marriage ceremony, that which is to be performed must certainly be observed.
For Brahmin women, receiving initiation from their husband is superior; however, if the husband is incapable, initiation from another is considered preferable. (53)
For women who are not Brahmins, it is not appropriate to derive their status from their husbands;
nor is it accepted that a non-Brahmin husband can serve as a spiritual teacher. (54)

A wife should maintain the same regard for her husband’s guru as she does for her own, and likewise, a husband should maintain the same regard for his wife’s guru as he does for his own; otherwise, they will certainly fall [from their status]. (55)
Since a wife is subject to the commands of her father-in-law, she is likewise subject to those of her husband; therefore, even when there is another guru, no contradiction arises for the woman. (56)
For that which has been taught by the Guru is not intended to be subsidiary to anything else;
indeed, only that which has been enjoyed by someone other than him could be considered subsidiary to another. (57)
Even though her husband is her guru, no fault shall accrue to the woman;
for his status as a father toward her is secondary (gauṇī), since it can never be primary (mukhyā). || 58 ||
He alone is figuratively designated as mother, father, and god;
yet by that much, the relationship between husband and wife is certainly not sublated. (59)
They have no authority over volitional intentions regarding meritorious deeds leading to heaven;
for their established authority over liberation cannot indeed be obstructed. (60)

Just as the notion of a deity is prescribed toward one's teacher and father, so too is it declared regarding the husband; this does not preclude [the worship of] deities. Consequently, the worship of deities is also commended for women.
The relationship of husband and wife is not eternal, for it is merely conceptualized; even such states as being a woman or a man are said to pertain only to this present life. (52)
This is neither female, nor male, nor indeed neuter;
whatever body it assumes, by that it is affected.
How can you obstruct the path leading to liberation for this slender woman, who has already renounced her femininity in this world as well as her status as a wife? 64.
Whether he has been meditated upon like a god or served like a guru, how could that fool save a virtuous woman without my worship? (65)
This vow must be observed by women as well:
"Wandering through the forest of existence and sinking into the ocean of suffering,
how can a fool who has not crossed over himself rescue another virtuous woman?"
Therefore, women must certainly observe this vow.
A woman who has not been purified by initiation is not fit for the service of her own initiated husband; therefore, she must first undergo initiation.
Whatever cooked food a woman who has not been consecrated by initiation prepares, that food indeed does not deserve to be offered to me. (68)
The water that a woman who has not been purified by initiation touches is not worthy of my rites of consecration and the like. (69)
For dependence is indeed declared for women regarding rites leading to heaven;
yet even in those pertaining to this world and for the sake of liberation, their independence is not obstructed.
Therefore, initiation must certainly be granted to women by the most excellent of the wise. (70)
Without contradicting her commitment to the emblems [of her order], she should maintain her own duties;
thus, a woman does not incur fault in matters such as service to her husband. (71)
While serving her husband, supporting her mother-in-law and others,
and protecting her sons and so forth, she must not forget her commitment to the [ascetic] marks.

Just as for a young mother performing household duties, her mind remains dependent on her child; so it is fitting for one who has been initiated. Therefore, domestic chores do not obstruct my service. (73)
Having become intent on the supreme state of the Liṅga, with her mind disciplined in devotion to Me,
she will, through service to her husband, attain union with Me by means of her lord.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, how can the touching of the linga, worship, and other rites be performed by one who is defiled by the arising of passion (rajas) and joined with the impurity of childbirth? (75)
Mahādeva said:
"The form of worship known as *arcā* (image worship) is indeed approved for householders;
Vedic mantras are not suitable for women, but Tantric ones are prescribed for them. (76)
Due to the limbs having been purified by initiation, the defects of dust and the like do not arise; thus, touching the *liṅga* is not considered defiled.
Even during times when there is dust or similar conditions, worship must be performed with diligent effort.
In calamities such as childbirth and the like, the interruption of worship does not constitute a fault. || 77 ||
The Goddess said:
"Is there a Vedic initiation or a Tantric initiation for women?
If it is Vedic, how could the mantras used in the worship be Tantric? (78)
If there is a mutual difference in initiation between a Tantric couple, how indeed could their success in all ritual acts be complete?
O Abode of Compassion, please sever this doubt of mine. (79)
Mahādeva said:

"Indeed, both initiations (dīkṣā) may be applied optionally for the wives of the twice-born. However, in the case of the Tantric initiation, the husband shall have authority, while for women [in general], it may be performed independently."
(38) Having placed the person first, there is an option between Vedic and Tantric initiation;
however, because the Vedic [initiation] depends on another [the wife], the distinction of initiation for the couple does not obstruct their compatibility. (81)
Now, having attained this authority, everything has been stated in brief, just as there is a distinction between the duties of men and women; what do you wish to hear from here on? (82)

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Greatness of Śāmbhava Initiation," in the Kriyāpāda of the Uttara-bhāga of the venerable *Kāraṇāgama*, within the dialogue between Pārvatī and Parameśvara.
The third chapter. The Goddess said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O Lord of the universe, salutations be unto you!
Now tell me the daily ritual (āhnika) for those who observe the Śāmbhava vow.
Mahādeva said:
O Daughter of the Mountain, my devotee, observing the daily rites of those who follow the Śāmbhava vow, should awaken during the Brāhma-muhūrta.
Touching his two eyes, he should meditate upon me as the desired Liṅga.

Following the path instructed by the guru, one should, with undistracted mind, contemplate me— either in my divine form or as formless— at the end of the twelve finger-breadths (dvādaśānta) or in the heart.
One should contemplate the teachings, their purposes, the afflictions arising therefrom, and one’s daily duties;
likewise, during the twilight hours, one should not perform the four activities: eating, attachment to women, study, or sleep. (4)
If a person falls asleep while the sun is rising or setting,
he should restrain his breath and recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
He who, at the time of dawn, beholds my devotee, the sacred ash, the rudrākṣa, myself, and the bilva tree, shall obtain his heart's desire. (6)
He who sees an heretic, a worldly seeker of rebirth, an outcast, a beggar, or a reviler of the gods at the time of dawn shall encounter misfortune.
Regarding the rules for purification: thereafter, a man should go from the village to the south-eastern intermediate direction;
having placed a water vessel there at a distance of one arrow-shot, he should proceed.
Having placed the *nivīta* and the *śivasūtra* upon his head with a cloth,
and having covered his head, he should look neither upwards nor downwards.
Facing the north, the twice-born man should direct his attention toward Soma, Agni, and Āditya;
then, with a concentrated mind, he may discharge urine and feces.
Therefore, endowed with purity of intention, one should diligently perform purification with earth and water; otherwise, ritual acts are fruitless.
Whether impure or pure, or even having reached any state whatsoever, he who remembers Virūpākṣa is pure both externally and internally. (12)
Having performed purification according to the rules and having thoroughly cleansed his hands and feet, he should offer water to me and then discharge the mouthfuls of water (gaṇḍūṣas). || 13 ||
Sitting with his topknot tied and his speech, mind, and body restrained,
he should place the sacred thread over his left shoulder and then perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
With his hands between his knees, touching the ground with the lower part of his body,
and facing north, he should sip water using the Brāhma-tīrtha.
When one has slept, sneezed, spat, changed clothes, shed tears,
or voided urine or feces, one who desires purity should perform ritual sipping of water (ācamana).

In the ritual touching of water as well as in bathing, and in all rites performed with self-restraint, the grasping of *kuśa* grass is prescribed; however, it is not recommended in rites pertaining to the ancestors (*paitṛka*).
Having sipped water for purification, one should always perform the cleansing of the teeth while facing east;
having consecrated the twig with the mantra beginning with "madhurī," [one should proceed]. 18.
"O Lord of the Forest, come to us for the sake of long life, strength, fame, luster, progeny, cattle, wealth, sacred knowledge, wisdom, and intelligence.
Having thus prayed with this mantra, one should likewise wash [the tree] with a branch. (19)
All thorny trees that produce milky sap are recommended for cleaning the teeth;
however, one should never perform the cleansing of the teeth with a branch of the bilva tree.
Having performed the rites of bathing and the cleansing of the teeth, one should then perform the morning ablution;
[one should bathe] in great rivers, natural pools dug by the gods, lakes, and ponds.
Pits, springs, and similar sources are recommended for the act of bathing.
Beauty, splendor, strength, purity, longevity, fortitude, freedom from disease, intelligence, and the destruction of bad dreams— these are proclaimed to be the qualities of ritual bathing.
The water that stands near my abode should be known as Śivagaṅgā; having bathed there, one shall obtain me.
One should perform the bath of impurity (malasnāna) and the bath by means of mantra;
specifically, one should perform the bath by approaching a river or similar body of water.
This has been declared as the bath of impurity; now listen to the bath by means of mantra.
Forming the resolve, reciting the hymns, performing the sprinkling (mārjana), the Aghamarṣaṇa rite, and the libation to the deities—this is said to be the fivefold bath. || 25 ||
Since that water is constantly inhabited by many aquatic creatures such as fish, frogs, and snakes, it therefore becomes defiled. (26)
The practitioner should take up the clay with the Astra-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, [shaped] as a square measuring one cubit on all sides. (27)
Having purified it with the Aghora-mantra, one should cast a third part into the eastern, southern, and northern [sections] by means of the Puruṣa-mantra. || 28 ||
One should consecrate each [item] with the Īśāna mantra;
having recited the Astra-Brahma-Śiva mantra, one should install them in order, starting from the east.
One should cast that portion which has been consecrated with the Astra-mantra into the ten directions;
one should cast that portion which has been consecrated with the Śiva-mantra into the middle of the sacred bathing place (tīrtha).
By means of the *phaṭ* syllable, the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), and likewise the *nārācamudrā*, there shall be the eradication of those subtle defects that exist in the water. || 31 ||
And with half of that which was recited for the Brahma-mantra, one should empower the limbs of oneself part by part:
the head, the face, the heart, the two feet, and the secret organ. (32)
Having touched [the water] with the remaining half [of the vessel], one should bathe repeatedly with water;
having thus performed the ritual sipping (upaspṛśya), one should likewise bathe in the midst of the Śiva-tīrtha.

Having performed the ritual bath with the limbs of Śiva-Brahman and the limbs of Vidyā, the wise practitioner should recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times with the five Brahmans and the limbs of Śiva.
Then, having made the water identical with Śiva by means of mantras whose essence is Śiva,
one should perform the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) with that water using the Saṃhitā mantras.
Bringing water consecrated with the Astra-mantra to the tip of the left nostril,
one should contemplate that the sin has been burnt by it as it enters within through the Iḍā-nāḍī.
Visualizing [the water] gone outside with the Piṅgalā [nāḍī], one should take water in the right hand and then visualize the personification of sin (pāpapūruṣa) therein. || 37 ||
Having visualized a diamond-stone (vajraśilā) on the left side, one should pour water upon it;
one should contemplate that the man of evil is pulverized—this is the *aghamarṣaṇa*. (38)
The wise one should satisfy the gods and others by the recitation of the root mantra;
with a pure mind, he should satisfy me, the Lord, and my own attendants. (39)
Having performed the ash-bath for the morning ablution, one should not smear the body with clay;
then, having discarded the wet garments, one should put on two clean washed cloths.
Having placed the chosen liṅga in his hand and having bathed it with water,
he— pure and with a purified inner self— should then perform the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna).
Having collected the ashes and consecrated them six times with the root mantra,
one should apply it to the head with the Īśāna mantra and likewise to the face with the Puruṣa mantra.
One should sprinkle the region of the heart with the Aghora mantra, the secret parts with the Vāmadeva mantra,
the feet with the Sadyojāta mantra, and all the limbs with the Praṇava itself.
This bath performed with ash is the supreme Agneya (fiery) rite.
One should smear all the limbs with dry ash while reciting the root mantra;
this is the *uddhūlana* (dusting), after which one should moisten it with water.
Having placed the palm of the left hand upon [the right], one should place a hexagon upon the ashes;
one should place the *praṇava* on its face, and the two *vāyavya* syllables on the two arms. (45)
Having written the syllable *śī* in the middle of the yantra and the two forms of *namaḥ* in the two feet, one should consecrate it six times with the root mantra. || 46 ||
On the head, on the forehead, on the two ears, on the two eyes, as well as on the nose, the mouth, the throat, and likewise on the pair of shoulders; || 47 ||
At the elbows, the wrists, the heart, both sides, the navel, the two secret parts, the thighs, the buttocks, and the knees. (48)
Having applied the triple mark of ashes (tripuṇḍra) on the two arms, the two feet, and likewise at the thirty-two locations, one should thereafter wear Rudrākṣa beads.
Regarding the wearing of rudrākṣas:
one should wear a single rudrākṣa on the crest-lock (śikhā), thirty on the head,
thirty-six on the neck, and sixteen on each of the two arms.
One should carry twelve [beads] on the wrist and five hundred on the shoulder;
for the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*), one should arrange a rosary consisting of one hundred and eight [beads]. (51)
One should wear two strings, three strings, or even five strings,
seven, or ten, around the region of the neck.
In the crown, in the earrings, in the ear-ornaments and necklaces, in the armlets and bracelets, and especially in the girdle; || 53 ||
Three hundred is said to be the lowest, five hundred the middle, and one thousand the highest; thus one should maintain [the practice] according to these divisions.

Then, in the worship of the twilight devotions (*sandhyopāsanapūjana*), one should perform the twilight rite preceded by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*); my own worship of the twilight is proclaimed as *sandhyopāsti*.
I am the mistress of the orb of the Sun, and Sāvitrī is my deity.
"If at the time of twilight another deity besides me is worshipped, four things of his perish—so they say: wisdom, fame, strength, and [longevity]. (56)

Therefore, I am to be worshipped at the three junctions of the day as the innermost essence, beyond the sun; I am designated by names such as Bharga and am the eternal impeller of the vital breath and the intellect.

O lady of excellent vows, at the rising of the dawn, at the rising of the sun, at the time of the morning union (saṅgava), at midday, and then in the evening and at midnight— I am to be worshipped during these six periods by those endowed with devotion through the highest [offerings]. (58)
Having respectfully performed the Śaiva twilight ritual (saṃdhyā) ending with the offering of water (arghya),
one should then perform the timely worship at the rising of the dawn.
With a restrained mind, one should recite the Sāvitrī mantra until sunrise,
and with undivided attention, one should worship the Sun, who is no other than myself.
Then, at sunrise, one should perform my worship as well as the fire-oblation (homa);
one should recite the six-syllabled mantra along with its ancillaries, and especially the Śrī Rudra and other hymns.
The sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) is superior to all sacrifices involving material substances (dravyayajña).
Having thus completed the sacrifice of recitation, one should pay homage to the guru and others.
Having divided the day into eight parts, one should thus conclude the first;
in the second part, however, one should practice the Vedas as well as the divine Āgamas.
One should cause the disciples to study the scriptures and awaken them to my true nature;
then, with devotion, one should perform the worship performed at the time of social gathering.
One should diligently gather sacrificial fuel such as *kuśa* grass for the purpose of the fire oblation (*homa*), as well as flowers, *bilva* leaves, *guggulu*, and other such substances. (65)
In the third part of the day, one should make an effort for the sake of supporting those dependent on him;
likewise, in the fourth part, one should fetch earth for the purpose of bathing.
Having prepared a sacred bathing place (śivatīrtha) and smeared his limbs with clay,
and having performed the midday bath and worshipped the two twilights (sandhyā),
the householder should then joyfully perform the five great sacrifices (pañcamahāyajña).
O daughter of the mountain, the five sacrifices are prescribed for the gods, the ancestors, the elemental beings, human beings,
and also for Brahman. (68)
Offering oblations with fuel and other materials into the fire is proclaimed as the sacrifice to the gods (devayajña);
giving water to the ancestors is declared to be the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña). || 69 ||
When one offers an oblation to the spirits, it is declared to be the sacrifice to beings (bhūtayajña);
when one bestows food upon Brahmins, that indeed is the sacrifice to men (manuṣyayajña);
and when one studies one's own Vedic recitation, it is called the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña).
(50) In the libation for the Agniṣvātta and other ancestors, the rite should be performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder;
however, in the libation for one's own paternal ancestors, that [same procedure] should not be performed again.
Then the midday worship should be performed—whether it be extensive or brief, or great according to one's capacity—with a self endowed with faith and devotion. (72)
Whether he be wise or foolish, beloved or even hateful—whosoever arrives at the conclusion of the worship, he is none other than I; of this there is no doubt. (73)
Indeed, that moving being who has come to one's house is superior even to me;
he is to be honored with food, drink, and the like, as well as by granting whatever he desires.
Having thus propitiated the Moving One (Viṣṇu) and enjoyed his grace, one should dwell in happiness with the mind fixed on Him, digesting that food.
Or he may recite hymns to me, or study the Purāṇas;
furthermore, until evening, he should exert effort for the sake of achieving the welfare of those dependent on him.
Then, having performed the evening duties, bathed, become pure, and performed the bath with ashes,
he should worship during the evening twilight and complete the rite of the fire-oblation.
Having performed the evening worship, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite.
Having performed my mid-night worship according to my ability, one should then worship with great devotion a guest who arrives in the evening. (78)
O Goddess, whatever sin may occur when a guest who has come during the day departs unhonored, that same sin becomes eightfold if he departs unhonored in the evening.
Therefore, having honored the guest who has arrived with the sun according to his own ability, the twice-born man,
after enjoying his favor, should also recite hymns to me.
Having occupied a bed pleasing to oneself, being pure and remembering me, one should lie down comfortably with the head toward the north, established in meditative concentration.
Thus, O beloved, I have described this collection of duties for the daily observance of my devotees among the twice-born, which is the means for attaining my state.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Rule for Daily Rituals," in the Kriyāpāda of the Uttara-bhāga of the Śrī-Kāraṇāgama, within the dialogue between Pārvatī and the Supreme Lord.
The Fourth Chapter. The Goddess said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O Lord of all, salutations be unto you!
O Lord, I have heard the daily recitation which bestows desired boons upon devotees.

The specific types of images for worship, the rules regarding the specific materials for their reception, the method for preparing colored powders, and likewise the preparation of drawing pencils; || 2 ||
O Blessed One, O ocean of compassion, I wish to hear about the appropriate leaves and flowers as well as their collection; please tell me this.
Mahādeva said:
Listen, O daughter of the mountain; there is nothing that should be hidden from you.
My worship is threefold: the light, the heavy, and likewise the great.
One who is capable should perform the threefold ritual of worship in its highest form, the great, and the medium;
one who is unable should perform it in its abbreviated form, both in the evening and at midday.
O lady of excellent vows, the times for eating are said to be morning and so forth;
one who is capable should perform worship at the three periods of the day, or even at all six periods. (6)
At sunrise, having bathed and offered the arghya water to Savitṛ,
a twice-born man should perform my worship and then recite the Sāvitrī mantra.
Until sunrise, one should subsequently attend upon the Sun;
having thus performed the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña), one should perform the worship at the time of sunrise.
One should perform [the rites] likewise during the *saṅgava* and at midday in due order;
having performed the evening twilight worship (*sāyaṃsandhyā*), one should likewise perform the evening worship (*sāyantanī*).
Beginning in the first watch of the night,
the householder, endowed with faith and devotion, should complete the worship at midnight.
Of the night, the first and last portions of the second watch are considered [the times for worship] for the householder;
for the ascetic, they are the end of the midnight worship and the beginning of the third watch.
Regarding the rules for the commencement [of the rite]: O sinless one, if an eclipse should occur during the first watch of the night,
then my midnight worship must be performed during the second watch.
When an eclipse occurs during the second or third watch [of the day],
a twice-born man should not eat after having set aside his food for worship;
furthermore, if he is observing the *nakta* vow, the specific rule is now stated.
When an eclipse occurs during the second or third watch,
my worship must be performed before that watch, not the meal.
During an eclipse of the moon, one should avoid the first watch for eating;
however, for those who subsist on the *naktam* fast, the time preceding that is recommended.
Even when the sun has been swallowed by Rāhu and has set, a fast is not prescribed;
for those who eat only at night must certainly observe the period of grace.
The *padmabhadratattvamaṇḍalas*—
namely, the *padma*, the *bhadra*, and likewise the *tattvamaṇḍala*— are proclaimed as the supreme sequence for the arrangement of vessels suitable for worship.
With white rice powder, an eight-petaled lotus should be formed. || 17 ||
One should draw eight lines extending toward the east and likewise eight lines across horizontally;
from this, a wheel of forty-nine squares is thus formed.
One should likewise place subtle lotuses within the thirty-six squares;
one should draw an eight-petaled lotus in the thirteen central spaces,
and furthermore, one should arrange the ten weapons around the mandala.
To the east, however, is the svastika and the conch; likewise, the lotus is in the southeast. To the south are the fly-whisk and the parasol; in the southwest is the five-cornered [figure]. (20)
In the west, the nāgabandha; in the northwest, the hexagon;
in the north, the ḍamaru; in the northeast, the trident and the octagon. || 21 ||
This Bhadra-maṇḍala, worthy for the placement of vessels for the worship of this Liṅga, has been described; it is dear to me, bestowing prosperity and supreme liberation. (22)
One should draw thirty-seven lines, both vertical and horizontal;
this results in a grid consisting of one thousand two hundred and ninety-six squares.
In the center of that, there is a wheel consisting of a lotus with thirty-six petals;
one should draw subtle lotuses in all the surrounding squares,
and the wise man should arrange the ten weapons around the mandala.

The supreme among the supreme is the mandala of reality (tattvamaṇḍala), which is declared to be the means for experiencing reality and for the arrangement of vessels for the worship of the chosen liṅga. || 25 ||
The lotus is prescribed for the [mandala] called Avasara, even when it is small;
one should also arrange the Bhadramandala and other such [mandalas] for the large [Avasara] and the others.
(56) One should light a single lamp during a short or intermediate occasion;
however, during a long or great occasion, one should light two or even four.
Three lustrations (nīrājana) are prescribed in the worship known as the "Occasion" (avasara).
The first is called "Beholding" (darśana), the second is called "Bathing" (majjana), and the third is indeed called the "Occasion"; thus one should perform the worship, O Dear One.
O fair-faced one, a set of nine lustrations (nīrājanā) has been briefly described:
the first is called Darśana, and the second is called Avasara. (29)
The third is called Majjana, while the fourth is named Māṅgalya;
the fifth shall be Karpūra, and the sixth is designated Śṛṅgāra.
The seventh is Mahāsaṃjña; here, the eighth is called Ānanda;
and this ninth is proclaimed by the name Asaṃkhyāta. || 31 ||
O you of beloved vows, in the great worship as well as in the worship of the Guru, there are indeed eleven [items], including that called Sānurāga and the one known as Tāmbūla.
Regarding the procedure for the wicks (*vartikā*):
here, three wicks are prescribed for that which is called the "Occasional" (*avasara*) rite;
nine or twelve wicks are declared for the "Light Worship" (*laghupūjana*).
Now, eighteen or thirty-six are prescribed for the worship of the Guru;
or the number according to the Ānava-krama, or likewise ninety-six.
Or one hundred and eight, or three hundred, or even a thousand; during my great worship, one should also light a wick-lamp. (35)
One should prepare a wick with thirty-six threads for my worship;
even with only three, the fruit shall be that which is declared for one hundred and eight.
I shall now describe the flowers suitable for worship—indeed, those flowers which are dear to me in ritual worship: the *nandyāvarta*, *śriyāvarta*, *karavīra*, and *baka*. (37)
Also the *droṇa*, *punnāga*, *mandāra*, and water-born *arkotpala* flowers;
as well as *lodhra*, *dhuttūra*, *nirguṇḍī*, *bilva*, *aśoka*, and *muni*. (38)
Among these, those of bright color are indeed exceedingly dear to me;
they are sattvic and truly bestow liberation. (39)
These are of the nature of passion (rājasa) and bring about the attainment of worldly enjoyments; those that are mixed and yellow in color indeed bestow both enjoyment and liberation.
O beloved, dark-colored items other than the blue lotus would be characterized by tamas; O lady of beautiful hips, they should never be employed in worship.
The Kadamba, the Campaka, the Punnāga, and likewise the Bṛhatī—by offering these to me in the spring, they shall grant the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. (42)
O lady of excellent complexion, the *pāṭalī*, the *mallikā*, and the *śatapatra* offered to me during the summer season would grant the fruit of the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice. (43)

The blue water-lily (*rājī*), the lotus (*ambuja*), the jasmine (*mallikā*), the blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), the white water-lily (*kahlāra*), the thorn-apple (*dhuttūra*), and the *jāti* flower— by being offered to me in autumn, these shall yield the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and bestow the merit of a Sattra sacrifice. (44)
O beloved, the Jāti, the blue lotus, and even the Karavīra grant the fruit of a hundred sacrifices; likewise, the Karṇikāra grants it during the winter season.
O fair-faced one, among flowers the āragvadha and droṇa are recommended, and among leaves the bael leaf is certainly most excellent for my worship. (46)
O Pārvatī, know that my worship performed with golden flowers such as the Droṇa and others, or with Bilva leaves, yields infinite fruit. (47)
In this world, there is no fault of being "used and discarded" (nirmālya) regarding leaves or flowers, even when they are made of gold; therefore, one should worship constantly with them. 48.
One should discard leaves, flowers, and fruits that have been brought by hand, brought on cloth, held in the hand of an *eraṇḍa* leaf, or brought by impure persons. (49)

A flower that has fallen to the ground, one that has been smelled, one devoid of its filaments, one infested with insects, one lacking its stalk, or one that is bruised is not fit for use in worship. (50)
Whether aquatic or terrestrial, one should place the leaves exactly as they were found;
likewise, one should place a bilva leaf facing downwards.
One should place the bilva fruit upon everything else, but nothing upon the bilva; one should place the sacred ash upon everything else, but nothing upon the sacred ash.
"Indeed, when my worship is performed in this manner, one certainly attains absolute liberation (kaivalya).
Everything has been told in brief; what do you wish to hear after this?"

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Rangavali and Other [Ornaments]," in the Kriyapada of the Uttara-bhaga of the glorious Karanagama, within the dialogue between Parvati and Paramesvara. || 4 ||
The Fifth Chapter. The Goddess said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, you who are devoted to the fivefold cosmic act!
O Lord of the Universe, O Soul of All, salutations be unto You again and again. || 1 ||
The specific characteristics of the vessels used for worship, as well as how the practitioner should conduct himself during the time of worship, are now described. (2)
Tell me entirely and without omission about the various substances for consecration and the rules for the worshiper— everything that is the cause of liberation for living beings.
Mahādeva said: "At the time of worship, how should one conduct oneself?
For from abundant ritual implements arises the purity of mind."
Only with a stainless mind may the worshiper partake of the fruit. || 4 ||
Through the presence of all necessary components, that worship becomes abundant;
when the worship is abundant, the devotee enjoys abundant prosperity.
Having gathered the materials required for worship and being seated comfortably on a pleasant seat, one should worship me with single-minded devotion, observing the prescribed restraints.
A person who sits down after having prepared the ritual requisites but then fails to perform the visualization with renewed effort—that deluded soul shall not partake in the fruit of the worship. (7)
Whether ignorant or wise, one should not personally summon the assembly;
for if he summons them from time to time, being fickle, he will not attain the fruit.
Having resolved to perform worship, the devotee should not become angry with the attendants;
for a worshipper who is inflamed by anger does not attain the presence [of the deity].
At the time of worship, one should avoid laziness, yawning, and sleep;
one should also avoid attachment to sense objects and instead act with devotion dedicated to me.
Whatever flower or leaf I have not obtained, one whose mind is offered to me should,
after carefully placing it nearby, offer it to me with the mind alone.
But he who, having resolved upon worship, is engaged in another task,
does not enjoy the fruit of the worship unless he keeps that task in mind.
If, during the midst of worship, someone—whether sent by one person or by many—is made to hasten me in my worship, that person's worship does not reach me. (13)
If summoned by the Guru, one should offer him worship; even when worship has been offered, if summoned again, one should carry out his command. (14)
Since I am the guru, O Queen of the Gods, no distinction exists between us; having realized this state of non-duality, one should observe his command. (15)
Whatever Vedic passage the learned man recites at the time of worship,
he should conclude by saying, "This has been uttered by me," through his own effort.
One should not sit near those who proclaim what is non-Vedic;
one should not offer a refusal, but should close both ears.
O Goddess, during the time of worship, one should not look upon a man who has been cast out.
Whatever unsurpassed Śaiva rite has been declared for the time of worship, one should perform it with every effort; however, if one is unable, one should have it performed [by another].
If a worshipper, while recollecting his worldly duties, hastens away,
he departs through an offense against Śiva to undergo the torments of Kālabhairava.
Even by merely remembering his deeds, he whose mind is fixed upon me goes to my own form on Kailāsa together with my attendants;
he rejoices there, and having no return [to this world], everything has been brought under his control.
"To whatever extent flowers, leaves, fruit, or water are acquired through effort, to that same extent I, Sadāśiva, am indeed the giver of their fruit. (21)

Greed for flowers, greed for leaves, and greed for vessels bring about fear. Therefore, with every effort, having procured a vessel, a leaf, and likewise a beautiful flower, one should worship the Liṅga according to the extent of one's available wealth.
O Śivā, having carefully prepared the characteristics of the vessels and so forth— specifically golden vessels and petals made of gold from flowers— I am to be worshipped.
If he is poor, he should indeed prepare a copper vessel instead of one made of silver. || 23 ||
One who is dispassionate should himself perform worship with a coconut as the vessel;
even worship with a golden vessel would not be equal to that.
A vessel fashioned from bilva wood is the most excellent of all;
there is nothing like that vessel in the world, nor does it exist anywhere upon the surface of the earth. (25)
Among vessels, that made of bilva wood is praiseworthy; among leaves, the bilva leaf is the most excellent.
Among flowers for the purpose of worship, the blue lotus is the very best of the best.
Having performed everything with non-ordinary mantras, one should offer it to me;
by worshipping with a pure disposition, one shall partake in the fruit as described. || 27 ||

One should personally worship with leaves, flowers, and unsurpassed fruits produced by one's own son, as well as wild flowers and leaves. One who performs the rite with items brought by a Śūdra or purchased falls into a low state.
One should worship me with devotion of mind using arka, droṇa, utpala, and other flowers, as well as bilva leaves, āragvadha leaves, sesame seeds, and unbroken rice grains. (29)
O Pārvatī, listen to the characteristics of the vessels for the *arghya* and other offerings used in worship:
namely, those called the general *arghya*, as well as the vessels for the feet (*pādārghya*) and for sipping water (*ācamana*).

O beloved, there are eleven vessels: those known as Tyāga, Jñāna, Ānanda, and Snānajala; three designated as Ādhāra for the water from the feet and the water of grace (prasāda); and the one called Śivakumbha.
Likewise, other vessels are indeed necessary for the sake of perfumes and the like, as well as for incense and especially for lamps. (32)
Having procured a bell, a conch, a mirror, an umbrella, a chowrie, and a fan, one should worship me in the form of the Liṅga. (33)
One should fashion the vessel named Śivakumbha with twenty palas;
one should fashion the vessel designated as the ordinary arghya with ten palas.
One should prepare the water for washing the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), and the water for sipping (ācamana) using seven and a half palas;
one may also prepare those which consist of renunciation, knowledge, and bliss using five palas. The vessels known as the *ādhāra* (support) should be made from a measure of two and a half palas.
One should likewise prepare a Śiva-pitcher and a common arghya-vessel;
it should have a large belly and be adorned with a mouth and neck.
One should cause the areas known as *pādya*, *arghya*, and *ācamana* to be made square;
the others, representing renunciation (*tyāga*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and bliss (*ānanda*), should be circular.
One should fashion a vessel for perfumes and other offerings as circular and endowed with eight petals;
and one should also make lamp vessels shaped like hand-drums (ḍamaru).
For the lustration ceremony, the wise man should prepare a three-faced, six-faced, or single-faced parasol adorned with a network of pearls.
But in the absence of gold and other such materials, one should have a vessel made from *kiṃśuka* wood, or from the horn of a rhinoceros, or from a sacrificial tree, or even from clay. (40)
(66) The procedure for worship:
On a riverbank or by a pond, at a site where Śiva is self-manifested, or even in a secluded place in one’s own home, one should perform sacrifice with a one-pointed mind. || 41 ||
One may offer one thousand and eight bilva fruits, or one hundred and eight,
or else a thousand droṇa flowers, or flowers produced from the arka plant.
Or one should worship with a thousand *āragvadha* flowers according to the rule, or even one hundred and eight, or by the number twenty-eight. (43)
One should not dwell with one who uses many words at the time of worship; rather,
my worshipper should cause the Purāṇas of Śiva alone to be heard, or listen to them himself, and should avoid worldly conversation and chatter.
Flowers produced in one's own garden are recommended for my worship.
One should avoid flowers belonging to a deity—that is, those from a divine grove—and one should not offer to me flowers intended for the worship of another. (45)
One should not request flowers from another person to offer them;
flowers obtained through begging are unfit for my worship. (46)
One should not offer incense and lamps without having first placed the food offering (naivedya);
after presenting the incense and lamps, one should not delay in offering the food.
(67) For the consecration, one should place divine substances into the flask:
cardamom, ushira root, cloves, musk, and that which is called "moon" (camphor).
Having ground these five substances into powder, one should cast them into the flask. || 48 ||
One should place siddhārtha, saffron, dūrvā grass, kuṣṭha, sandalwood ash, camphor, and flowers into the vessel for the water for the feet.
One should place siddhārtha seeds, tips of kuśa grass, barley, rice, and sesame, as well as sandalwood, ashes, and flowers, into the arghya vessel.
One should place triphalā, jāti, karpūra, kuṣṭha, and kośīra,
as well as ashes, sandalwood, and flowers, into the vessel for sipping water (ācamana);
one should also deposit the ashes, sandalwood, and flowers into other vessels.
One should fill the vessel of renunciation with lukewarm water, the vessel of knowledge with water mixed with sandalwood,
and likewise the vessel of bliss with cool water.
Closing both eyes, one should practice meditation perfectly.
